decision.what_is_decided: Whether arbitrary tool-result text contains instructions aimed at an AI that will read it, which type that text is, and whether to flag it as untrusted.

inputs.name: content
inputs.source: Caller-supplied text, truncated before the ask
inputs.role: The free-form text Jev must interpret for AI-directed instructions

inputs.name: source
inputs.source: Optional origin label, else the tool name
inputs.role: Tells Jev where the text came from

inputs.name: user_task
inputs.source: Optional task string from the caller
inputs.role: Extra context for judging the content against the user's work

inputs.name: tool
inputs.role: Exact skip: some tools never scan

inputs.name: injectP
inputs.role: Exact cutoff on directed probability for flagging

outcomes: flagged injection or canary (or unknown kind)
not flagged (discussion, benign, or low probability)
decision.downstream_action: Returns flagged, kind, probability, and a message telling the agent to treat flagged text as untrusted and not follow it. Callers are not in this file.

jev_questions.what_it_asks: Whether the content addresses an AI agent and tries to instruct it, versus ordinary data, code, or talk about injection.
Which label best fits any AI-directed text: injection, canary, discussion, or benign.

semantic_ambiguity.evidence: Criteria split actual instructions to the reading agent from docs, tutorials, tests, and detection code that only discuss injection.

context_dependence.evidence: Ask state includes source and optional user task; the same wording can be an attack or a write-up depending on framing and who it addresses.

deterministic_expressibility.evidence: Input is unbounded natural language and code; injection phrasing is adversarial. A later keyword excerpt is only for highlighting, not this verdict.

judgment_required.evidence: Noul true/false and four-way choice rest on intent: aimed at the reading agent, trap, discussion, or none.

rule_stability.evidence: Comment notes the same injection questions would flag all legitimate skill/rule files; thresholds are env-tunable.

risk_or_policy_component.evidence: File states code owns policy and Jev answers narrow questions; flagging drives untrusted-content handling.

natural_language_understanding.evidence: The scanned payload is free-form content of at least a minimum length, not a structured field.

decision_complexity.evidence: Two semantic questions then a simple probability-and-kind rule; hardness is interpretation, not control flow.

why_jev_hypotheses.evidence: SCAN_QUESTIONS ask whether text addresses an AI and tries to instruct it, and which description fits, which is meaning not parsing (src/guard.js:4-26,154).
Instructions explicitly separate hidden directives from content that only discusses prompt injection, tutorials, tests, or detection code (src/guard.js:7-15,23).
Kind is a four-way choice: injection, canary, discussion, benign; flagging keeps injection, canary, and unknown (src/guard.js:17-25,155-157).
Directed is noul with true/false criteria about whether an instruction is aimed at an AI that reads the content (src/guard.js:5-15).
Opening comment: code owns policy, Jev answers narrow questions. Jev applies security criteria; scanContent then applies injectP (src/guard.js:1,111-114,154-157).
The scan is a threat classification of untrusted tool output; flagged message treats the text as an attempt to steer the agent (src/guard.js:148-162).
Classification depends on whether wording is aimed at the reading agent versus documenting attacks; source and optional user_task are passed in (src/guard.js:8-11,154).
Arbitrary truncated content; comment that injection questions would flag all instruction files shows keyword/intent rules misfire (src/guard.js:29-31,154,215-218).
Flag cutoff is an env probability; legitimate vs planted instruction files needed measured thresholds elsewhere in this file (src/guard.js:111-114,157,165-168).
Text is any tool result above a length floor, possibly truncated with the tail kept because injections hide at the end (src/guard.js:152-154,215-218).
Skip lists depend on tool; Jev state includes source and optional user_task; instruction files use a different question set (src/guard.js:29-31,151-154).
Comment avoids Jev round-trips for some tools; excerpt uses keyword lines only after the fact, not as the classifier (src/guard.js:101-107,195-199).

not_reasons.note: Security-relevant, but Jev is chosen for interpreting text; skips show they avoid Jev when a cheap exact check suffices.
They skip short text and listed tools specifically to avoid a Jev round-trip; cost is a reason not to call Jev.
scanContent is a short wrapper: skips, one ask, then a threshold.
Only skip conditions and a boolean flagged combination; no large branch tree.
This is a shared adapter check, but importance is not evidenced as the reason Jev is used instead of rules.
The code is simple; the hard part is the semantic questions, not intricate logic.

observed.claim: scanContent sends truncated content, source, and optional user task to ask with SCAN_QUESTIONS.

evidence.observation: ask is invoked with that state object and SCAN_QUESTIONS.

observed.claim: Jev is asked a yes/no about AI-directed instructions and a four-way kind label.

evidence.observation: SCAN_QUESTIONS defines directed as noul and kind as choice among injection, canary, discussion, benign.

observed.claim: After Jev returns, flagging is an exact probability cutoff plus kind membership.

evidence.observation: flagged if directed p meets injectP and kind is injection, canary, or unknown.

observed.claim: Some inputs never reach Jev: listed tools and short text.

evidence.observation: Returns null for never-external or skip-scan tools and text below MIN_SCAN_CHARS.
Comments and sets mark tools not worth a Jev round-trip and a minimum scan length.

observed.claim: The file states code owns policy and Jev answers narrow questions.

evidence.observation: Top comment describes that split for every adapter.

inferred.claim: Jev is here because telling an attack on the reading agent from discussion, tests, or ordinary data in free text is a judgment, not a parse.

evidence.observation: Directed criteria require deciding if an instruction is aimed at an AI that reads the content.
Kind criteria contrast behavior-changing injections and canaries with talk-about-injection and no AI-directed text.

inferred.claim: Keyword rules are treated as too crude for this verdict; they are used only to pick excerpt lines later.

evidence.observation: Comment that injection questions would flag all skill/rule files, so a different question set is used there.
excerpt uses a hot-word line filter, separate from scanContent's ask.

unknown: Why the developer chose Jev versus another classifier or model API.
How each caller acts on flagged (block, warn, store).
Whether regex or list-based scanners were tried and failed.
Real-world false-positive rates for this scan.

deterministic_alternative.what_rules_would_need: A catalog of injection and canary phrasings, plus rules to ignore security docs, tests, and detection code, covering hidden, multilingual, and end-of-file payloads in arbitrary tool output.
deterministic_alternative.adequacy: Fragile to impossible: attackers vary wording; discussion of injection looks like injection; the file already notes the same questions misfire on legitimate instruction files.
